screens.title: Introduction to Concurrency and Threads
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we open the door to concurrency and threads in Java. Concurrency means parts of a program can make progress independently and appear to run at the same time by interleaving execution, while parallelism is the literal simultaneous execution on multiple processor cores. You will learn why multithreading matters for responsiveness, throughput, and natural modeling of independent tasks. Practically, you will see two primary ways Java creates threads: by implementing the Runnable interface and by extending the Thread class, and why implementing Runnable is generally preferred because of Java’s single inheritance. We will also examine how to start threads correctly using start(), how Thread. sleep can be interrupted, and how to handle InterruptedException responsibly. A concrete outcome of this chapter is the ability to write simple multithreaded programs and reason about interleaved output. Along the way we will point out common mistakes, such as calling run() instead of start(), and how to observe thread names to confirm concurrent behavior. By the end you will be able to create worker threads, simulate batch processing, and make deliberate design choices about task structure. Consider how a responsive UI or a server handling multiple clients relies on these exact ideas you are about to learn.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Introduction to Concurrency and Threads

Introduction to Concurrency and Threads

Understand how Java runs multiple activities without freezing your program, and learn the two primary ways to define work for a thread.

In this lesson
Concurrency vs parallelism, thread creation, start vs run, sleep and interruptions.
Hands-on
Build a BatchProcessor that runs multiple worker threads and observe interleaving.
Why it matters
Keep UIs responsive and speed up data processing on multi-core systems.
Explore Key Topics
Concurrency vs Parallelism
Interleaving on one core versus simultaneous execution on multiple cores.
Creating Threads
Implement Runnable or extend Thread; Runnable is usually more flexible.
Interruption & Sleep
Handle InterruptedException and restore status when needed.
Visual concept
Task blueprint becomes a Runnable; Thread executes it. Multiple threads interleave output.
Runnable
Defines the work via run()
Thread
Executes a Runnable when start() is called
Quick tip
Always call start() to create a new thread. Calling run() just runs the code on the current thread.

screens.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism
screens.narratorSegment: Start by distinguishing two words that are often used together: concurrency and parallelism. Concurrency is about the structure of a program: different parts can make progress independently and their executions can overlap in time. On a single-core system this usually looks like interleaving, where the scheduler gives each task a turn. Parallelism is a stronger claim: multiple tasks literally run at the same exact instant, which requires multiple C P U cores. A concrete example: a single-core laptop with two running threads will switch between them so both make progress — that is concurrency by interleaving. The same two threads on a dual-core C P U could run simultaneously, yielding parallelism. A common misconception is to assume concurrency always implies a speedup; it does not automatically. Concurrency makes programs more responsive or easier to model, but only parallelism on multiple cores provides true simultaneous execution for compute-bound tasks. Consider a UI that delegates a long download to another thread — this is concurrency that improves responsiveness even without parallelism. Closing question: for the task you are about to build, do you need responsiveness or raw parallel compute, and how does that choice change your design?

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: Concurrency is about independent progress and interleaving; parallelism is simultaneous execution on multiple cores.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Concurrency vs Parallelism
Concurrency

Interleaving and independent progress

Parts of a program can make progress independently; on single cores they interleave execution under a scheduler.

  • • Improves responsiveness by moving blocking work off the main thread.
  • • Useful for modeling independent activities like handling multiple requests.
  • • Does not guarantee faster completion for CPU-bound work on a single core.
Example
A UI thread delegates a file download to a worker thread so the interface stays responsive even while data transfers proceed.
Parallelism

True simultaneous execution

Multiple tasks execute at the exact same instant on separate processor cores, providing potential speedup for compute-bound work.

  • • Requires multi-core hardware to run tasks simultaneously.
  • • Dividing work across cores can reduce wall-clock time for large datasets.
  • • Needs safe handling of shared resources to avoid race conditions.
Example
Splitting a large data set into chunks and processing chunks on separate cores to lower overall runtime.
Key takeaway

Choose concurrency for responsiveness and architecture. Choose parallelism when you need multi-core speed for CPU-bound work.

Check your understanding
Do you need responsiveness or raw parallel compute for your task? That answer guides whether you prioritize task separation or multi-core partitioning.

screens.title: What is a Thread?
screens.narratorSegment: A thread is the smallest unit of execution that the operating system scheduler can run. In Java every program starts with a single main thread that begins program execution, and you can create additional threads to perform work concurrently. Think of a thread as a lightweight worker that has its own execution stack and can run code independently of other threads. A concrete example: when you launch a simple Java program, the main thread reads input and can create worker threads to process data; those workers run independently and may complete at different times. A common misconception is to confuse a thread with a process; processes are heavier and have separate memory spaces, while threads within a process share memory. Sharing memory is powerful but risky — it introduces potential race conditions if multiple threads modify the same data without coordination. The practical takeaway is that threads let you structure work as independent activities, but careful design or later synchronization primitives are required when they share resources. Try naming your threads in small examples to make their output easier to follow.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › What is a Thread?
Definition

Thread: a lightweight sub-process

A thread has its own execution stack and shares memory with other threads in the same process.

Main thread
Starts program execution automatically.
Worker threads
Created by program to perform concurrent tasks.
Concrete example
A GUI program uses the main thread for UI events and spawns worker threads to download or process files so the UI remains responsive.
Key takeaway
Threads let multiple activities progress independently, but shared memory needs careful coordination.

screens.title: Create a Thread by Implementing Runnable
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing Runnable is a common and flexible way to define work for a thread. The Runnable interface declares a single run method which contains the task logic. In practice you create a class that implements Runnable, implement run to perform the work, construct a Thread with that Runnable, and call start on the Thread. Calling start asks the JVM to create a new execution context and invoke run on that new thread; this is what truly begins concurrent execution. A concrete example is a small task that prints progress steps and sleeps briefly to simulate work; two such tasks wrapped in separate Thread objects will produce interleaved output when started. A frequent misconception is that calling run directly runs the code in a new thread; it does not. Calling run simply executes the method in the current thread. Proper handling of InterruptedException inside run is also important: catch interruptions, optionally restore the interrupted status with Thread. currentThread(). interrupt(), and exit if the task should stop. Practice: implement the sample Runnable, start two threads with meaningful names, and observe the printed thread names to confirm concurrency. What did you see in the interleaving?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Create a Thread by Implementing Runnable
Code example
public class MyRunnableTask implements Runnable {
  private String taskName;

  public MyRunnableTask(String name) {
    this.taskName = name;
  }

  @Override
  public void run() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
      System.out.println(taskName + ": Running step " + i + " on thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
      try {
        Thread.sleep(100); // Simulate some work
      } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        System.out.println(taskName + ": Interrupted!");
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // Restore the interrupted status
        return; // Exit the run method
      }
    }
    System.out.println(taskName + ": Finished!");
  }
}
Explanation
  • • The class implements Runnable and provides run() with the task logic.
  • • Create a Thread by passing a Runnable instance to its constructor and give it a name for clarity.
  • • Call start() to begin execution in a new thread; do not call run() directly.
  • • Sleep simulates work and can throw InterruptedException; catch it and restore the status if appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Implement Runnable to define tasks and use Thread to execute them; handling interruptions makes tasks cooperative and safe to stop.

screens.title: Create a Thread by Extending Thread
screens.narratorSegment: Extending the Thread class is the alternative way to define a thread in Java. You create a subclass of Thread and override its run method with the task logic. Then you instantiate your subclass and call start to ask the JVM to run that run method in a new thread. This approach works, but it couples your class with Thread and prevents it from extending any other class because Java allows only single inheritance. A concrete example from the chapter shows a custom Thread subclass that names itself via the Thread constructor, performs work in a loop, calls Thread. sleep to simulate work, and handles InterruptedException by restoring the interrupted status and returning. Use this approach when the class itself logically represents a thread, but prefer Runnable for task objects that should remain independent and reusable. A common misconception is thinking extending Thread is always simpler; in many designs it reduces flexibility. Consider whether your task needs to inherit behavior from a different base class before choosing to extend Thread. Create a Thread by Extending Thread means extending thread defines behavior in the subclass but reduces flexibility due to single inheritance; prefer runnable for reusable task objects.. In practical terms, when to use thread subclassing and its limitations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Create a Thread by Extending Thread
Code example
public class MyThreadClass extends Thread {
  private String threadName;

  public MyThreadClass(String name) {
    super(name);
    this.threadName = name;
  }

  @Override
  public void run() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
      System.out.println(threadName + ": Running step " + i + " on thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
      try {
        Thread.sleep(120);
      } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        System.out.println(threadName + ": Interrupted!");
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        return;
      }
    }
    System.out.println(threadName + ": Finished!");
  }
}
Explanation & trade-offs
  • • Subclassing Thread bundles the task and the thread control in one class.
  • • Use when the class conceptually is a thread, but avoid if you need to extend another base class.
  • • Like Runnable, handle InterruptedException and restore the interrupted status if you rethrow or stop.
Pro tip
Favor Runnable for tasks and composition. Reserve Thread extension for special cases where extension is required.

screens.title: start() vs run(): a Common Mistake
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most common beginner mistakes is calling run directly on a Thread instance instead of calling start. start tells the JVM to create a new thread and then invokes run inside that new thread. Calling run simply executes the run method in the current thread, so no new thread is created and execution remains sequential. For example, consider code that creates a Thread with a Runnable and then calls thread. run(). The printed output will appear just like a simple method call on the main thread, and you will not see interleaving. A simple mental check before running your program is to search for start() calls: if you meant to create a new concurrent activity, use start. Another misconception is believing that run and start are interchangeable; they are not. When debugging, naming threads and watching their printed thread names will reveal whether they ran in separate threads. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › start() vs run(): a Common Mistake
What start() does

start() asks the JVM to create a new thread of execution. The JVM sets up a new context and invokes run() on that separate thread, enabling concurrent execution.

Example outcome
Multiple thread names appear interleaved in output, indicating actual concurrency.
What run() does

run() is a normal method invocation. It executes the task’s code on the current thread and does not spawn a new thread.

Common mistake
Calling run instead of start causes sequential behavior and confusion about concurrency.
Check

If you expect a new thread, ensure the code calls start(). If you see sequential output, search for an accidental run() call.

screens.title: Thread.sleep and InterruptedException
screens.narratorSegment: Thread. sleep pauses the currently executing thread for a specified number of milliseconds. It is a convenient way to simulate work or to wait without busy looping, but calling sleep can throw InterruptedException when another thread interrupts the sleeping thread. Handling InterruptedException properly is important for cooperative cancellation. The recommended pattern is to catch the exception, do any necessary cleanup, restore the interrupted status by calling Thread. currentThread(). interrupt(), and then return if the task should stop. This lets higher-level code detect that the thread was interrupted. A concrete example: a worker that sleeps between processing steps may receive an interrupt request to stop early; catching InterruptedException and returning cleans up and ends the run method quickly. A common pitfall is to swallow the exception and continue as if nothing happened; that hides the interruption and prevents timely shutdown. Always decide whether to stop or continue and communicate that decision by preserving the interrupted status when appropriate. In practical terms, what sleep does and how to handle interruptions safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Thread.sleep and InterruptedException
How sleep works

Sleep suspends the currently executing thread for the given time. During sleep the thread can be interrupted, which raises InterruptedException.

Handling pattern
try {
  Thread.sleep(milliseconds);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
  // Optional cleanup
  Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore status
  return; // stop the task
}
Concrete scenario
A batch worker sleeps between items. If the system requests shutdown, interrupting the worker lets it stop promptly and safely.
Key takeaway
Treat InterruptedException as a signal to stop or to clean up; do not silently ignore it.

screens.title: BatchProcessor: a Multithreaded Example
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity ties together the concepts you've learned. You will create a BatchProcessor class that implements Runnable, accepts a batchId and numberOfItems, loops through items while printing progress, sleeps briefly to simulate work, and handles interruptions. In main you create three BatchProcessor instances and wrap each in a Thread with a meaningful name, then start all threads. When you run the program you will see interleaved output from different processors and the main thread. Observing thread names in output confirms concurrent behavior. The instructional template provided shows the structure and leaves the run method implementation as the main exercise. A common misconception is expecting deterministic ordering; because scheduling is non-deterministic, the exact interleaving will vary each run. screens.title: Runnable vs Thread: When to Prefer Which
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between implementing Runnable and extending Thread affects code design. Implementing Runnable cleanly separates the unit of work from thread control. This separation allows your task classes to extend other classes if needed and keeps task logic reusable: the same Runnable can be executed by different thread pools or threaded wrappers. Extending Thread embeds the task into a thread instance and can be appropriate if the class conceptually represents a thread, but it blocks inheritance from other classes. A concrete, practical rule from the chapter is to prefer Runnable in most cases because of Java’s single inheritance model. Another important consideration is composition: with Runnable you can pass tasks into executors and thread pools in higher-level concurrency frameworks. A common misconception is that Runnable is always lighter-weight than Thread; the real benefit is design flexibility. When deciding, ask whether your task needs to reuse another base class or be run by different executors. The closing question is: will your task be a reusable unit of work or a specialized thread object? screens.title: Common Errors and Debugging Tips
screens.narratorSegment: Threaded programs introduce distinct classes of bugs that are uncommon in single-threaded code. Begin debugging by checking simple syntactic mistakes: ensure start() is used instead of run(), and verify that thread names are set for clearer logs. Next, handle InterruptedException correctly; never silently swallow it unless you have a deliberate reason. Another common issue is UI freezing because long-running tasks run on the main thread; move blocking or C P U-heavy work to worker threads to keep interfaces responsive. Race conditions and shared-state bugs are out of scope for this chapter, but be aware that shared mutable data across threads requires synchronization or higher-level concurrency constructs. Practical debugging tips include adding thread names to log lines, using small sleep intervals to make interleaving visible, and running the program multiple times to observe non-deterministic behavior. If you see inconsistent behavior, try simplifying the workload to reproduce the issue deterministically. Final question: when you see strange output ordering, is it a scheduler effect, an accidental run() call, or a shared-state race? Start with the simplest possibility and work up. screens.title: Core Components of a Simple Multithreaded App
screens.narratorSegment: A simple multithreaded application typically contains three core components: the task definition, the threads that execute tasks, and simple coordination points. The task definition is usually a Runnable implementation or a Thread subclass that contains the run method and the logic to perform. Coordination points include sleep, interruption, and possibly shared flags or queues; these let threads yield, wait, or be asked to stop. For example, in the BatchProcessor activity the Runnable is the processing logic, the Thread objects are named processors, and Thread. sleep simulates per-item work while InterruptedException provides a way to stop. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we open the door to concurrency and threads in Java. Concurrency means parts of a program can make progress independently and appear to run at the same time by interleaving execution, while parallelism is the literal simultaneous execution on multiple processor cores. You will learn why multithreading matters for responsiveness, throughput, and natural modeling of independent tasks. Practically, you will see two primary ways Java creates threads: by implementing the Runnable interface and by extending the Thread class, and why implementing Runnable is generally preferred because of Java’s single inheritance. We will also examine how to start threads correctly using start(), how Thread. sleep can be interrupted, and how to handle InterruptedException responsibly. A concrete outcome of this chapter is the ability to write simple multithreaded programs and reason about interleaved output. Along the way we will point out common mistakes, such as calling run() instead of start(), and how to observe thread names to confirm concurrent behavior. By the end you will be able to create worker threads, simulate batch processing, and make deliberate design choices about task structure. Consider how a responsive UI or a server handling multiple clients relies on these exact ideas you are about to learn.

By the end of these lessons you will understand the foundational vocabulary and practical steps to create simple concurrent programs in Java. You will clearly distinguish concurrency from parallelism and explain when tasks merely interleave versus when they truly execute at the same time on multiple cores. You will be able to describe threads and the main thread that starts a Java application, and you will know two ways to create threads: implementing Runnable and extending Thread. Importantly, you will practice creating and starting threads, observe interleaved output, and reason about why implementing Runnable is usually the better design choice because it lets your class extend something else if needed. This screen groups objectives into four measurable skills: conceptual understanding, explanation of benefits, practical thread creation, and writing basic thread-starting code. Each objective connects to verified competency milestones you can use to confirm your progress. As you move forward, refer back to these objectives to check that you can not only read examples, but also write and reason about multithreaded Java programs.

These next objectives focus on hands-on skills and defensive programming when you write threads. You will identify the core components of a simple multithreaded application: the task definition, the thread that executes it, and coordination points like sleep and interruption. You will implement the Runnable interface in a real class and pass instances to Thread objects, giving each thread a descriptive name for easier observation. Another objective is to correctly handle InterruptedException when calling Thread. sleep or other blocking operations and to restore the interrupted status when appropriate. Finally, you'll learn a design guideline: prefer implementing Runnable so your class can extend another base class if needed. Each objective includes a verified milestone so you can test yourself: run a batch processor with multiple threads, confirm their names appear in output, and demonstrate proper interruption handling. As you practice, keep an eye out for common mistakes such as calling run() instead of start() and leaving long-running work on the main thread, which can freeze user interfaces.

Start by distinguishing two words that are often used together: concurrency and parallelism. Concurrency is about the structure of a program: different parts can make progress independently and their executions can overlap in time. On a single-core system this usually looks like interleaving, where the scheduler gives each task a turn. Parallelism is a stronger claim: multiple tasks literally run at the same exact instant, which requires multiple C P U cores. A concrete example: a single-core laptop with two running threads will switch between them so both make progress — that is concurrency by interleaving. The same two threads on a dual-core C P U could run simultaneously, yielding parallelism. A common misconception is to assume concurrency always implies a speedup; it does not automatically. Concurrency makes programs more responsive or easier to model, but only parallelism on multiple cores provides true simultaneous execution for compute-bound tasks. Consider a UI that delegates a long download to another thread — this is concurrency that improves responsiveness even without parallelism. Closing question: for the task you are about to build, do you need responsiveness or raw parallel compute, and how does that choice change your design?

A thread is the smallest unit of execution that the operating system scheduler can run. In Java every program starts with a single main thread that begins program execution, and you can create additional threads to perform work concurrently. Think of a thread as a lightweight worker that has its own execution stack and can run code independently of other threads. A concrete example: when you launch a simple Java program, the main thread reads input and can create worker threads to process data; those workers run independently and may complete at different times. A common misconception is to confuse a thread with a process; processes are heavier and have separate memory spaces, while threads within a process share memory. Sharing memory is powerful but risky — it introduces potential race conditions if multiple threads modify the same data without coordination. The practical takeaway is that threads let you structure work as independent activities, but careful design or later synchronization primitives are required when they share resources. Try naming your threads in small examples to make their output easier to follow.

Implementing Runnable is a common and flexible way to define work for a thread. The Runnable interface declares a single run method which contains the task logic. In practice you create a class that implements Runnable, implement run to perform the work, construct a Thread with that Runnable, and call start on the Thread. Calling start asks the JVM to create a new execution context and invoke run on that new thread; this is what truly begins concurrent execution. A concrete example is a small task that prints progress steps and sleeps briefly to simulate work; two such tasks wrapped in separate Thread objects will produce interleaved output when started. A frequent misconception is that calling run directly runs the code in a new thread; it does not. Calling run simply executes the method in the current thread. Proper handling of InterruptedException inside run is also important: catch interruptions, optionally restore the interrupted status with Thread. currentThread(). interrupt(), and exit if the task should stop. Practice: implement the sample Runnable, start two threads with meaningful names, and observe the printed thread names to confirm concurrency. What did you see in the interleaving?

Extending the Thread class is the alternative way to define a thread in Java. You create a subclass of Thread and override its run method with the task logic. Then you instantiate your subclass and call start to ask the JVM to run that run method in a new thread. This approach works, but it couples your class with Thread and prevents it from extending any other class because Java allows only single inheritance. A concrete example from the chapter shows a custom Thread subclass that names itself via the Thread constructor, performs work in a loop, calls Thread. sleep to simulate work, and handles InterruptedException by restoring the interrupted status and returning. Use this approach when the class itself logically represents a thread, but prefer Runnable for task objects that should remain independent and reusable. A common misconception is thinking extending Thread is always simpler; in many designs it reduces flexibility. Consider whether your task needs to inherit behavior from a different base class before choosing to extend Thread. Create a Thread by Extending Thread means extending thread defines behavior in the subclass but reduces flexibility due to single inheritance; prefer runnable for reusable task objects.. In practical terms, when to use thread subclassing and its limitations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

One of the most common beginner mistakes is calling run directly on a Thread instance instead of calling start. start tells the JVM to create a new thread and then invokes run inside that new thread. Calling run simply executes the run method in the current thread, so no new thread is created and execution remains sequential. For example, consider code that creates a Thread with a Runnable and then calls thread. run(). The printed output will appear just like a simple method call on the main thread, and you will not see interleaving. A simple mental check before running your program is to search for start() calls: if you meant to create a new concurrent activity, use start. Another misconception is believing that run and start are interchangeable; they are not. When debugging, naming threads and watching their printed thread names will reveal whether they ran in separate threads. Closing question: when you read code that invokes run directly, ask whether the author intended concurrency or a simple synchronous method call. start() vs run(): a Common Mistake means call start() to spawn a new thread. calling run() executes task code on the current thread and does not create concurrency.. Thread. sleep pauses the currently executing thread for a specified number of milliseconds. It is a convenient way to simulate work or to wait without busy looping, but calling sleep can throw InterruptedException when another thread interrupts the sleeping thread. Handling InterruptedException properly is important for cooperative cancellation. The recommended pattern is to catch the exception, do any necessary cleanup, restore the interrupted status by calling Thread. currentThread(). interrupt(), and then return if the task should stop. This lets higher-level code detect that the thread was interrupted. A concrete example: a worker that sleeps between processing steps may receive an interrupt request to stop early; catching InterruptedException and returning cleans up and ends the run method quickly. A common pitfall is to swallow the exception and continue as if nothing happened; that hides the interruption and prevents timely shutdown. Always decide whether to stop or continue and communicate that decision by preserving the interrupted status when appropriate. Choosing between implementing Runnable and extending Thread affects code design. Implementing Runnable cleanly separates the unit of work from thread control. This separation allows your task classes to extend other classes if needed and keeps task logic reusable: the same Runnable can be executed by different thread pools or threaded wrappers. Extending Thread embeds the task into a thread instance and can be appropriate if the class conceptually represents a thread, but it blocks inheritance from other classes. A concrete, practical rule from the chapter is to prefer Runnable in most cases because of Java’s single inheritance model. Another important consideration is composition: with Runnable you can pass tasks into executors and thread pools in higher-level concurrency frameworks. A common misconception is that Runnable is always lighter-weight than Thread; the real benefit is design flexibility. When deciding, ask whether your task needs to reuse another base class or be run by different executors. The closing question is: will your task be a reusable unit of work or a specialized thread object? A simple multithreaded application typically contains three core components: the task definition, the threads that execute tasks, and simple coordination points. The task definition is usually a Runnable implementation or a Thread subclass that contains the run method and the logic to perform. Coordination points include sleep, interruption, and possibly shared flags or queues; these let threads yield, wait, or be asked to stop. Let's summarize three essential concepts to carry forward. First, concurrency allows different parts of a program to make progress independently; on single-core systems this usually appears as interleaving. Second, parallelism means tasks literally execute at the same time on multiple cores, and that difference matters when optimizing compute-bound work. Third, threads are the runtime units of concurrency in Java: the main thread starts automatically and you create additional threads to run tasks concurrently. Keep these definitions clear as you design programs: concurrency is about structuring independent activities, parallelism is about hardware-enabled simultaneous execution, and threads are how Java expresses concurrent work. A final set of concise, actionable definitions will help you while coding. First, the Runnable interface is a task blueprint: implement run to define what the task does and pass the instance to a Thread to execute it. Second, the start method on Thread is the correct way to create a new thread of execution; start triggers the JVM to run run in a distinct context. Third, InterruptedException is the mechanism used when a sleeping or blocked thread is requested to stop; handle it by cleaning up and restoring the interrupted status if you exit. These three terms are the ones you will reference most as you write small concurrent programs: use Runnable to define work, call start to run work concurrently, and treat InterruptedException as a respectful request to stop.
